terms.grammar: adjective used as a pronoun, in the gender of the noun understood; gen. nūllīus, dat. nūllī
terms.comment: Latin keeps the gender of what is meant: of footprints (vestīgia), nūlla; of holidays (fēriae), nūllae. Of two, “neither” is neuter (see neither); of a quantity, “none (of it)” is nihil (see nothing). A bare answer “none” is often the verb repeated with nōn.

terms.gloss: none (of persons): none of us, none of them
terms.grammar: pronoun; in classical Latin gen. nūllīus, abl. nūllō
evidence: Sen. Ep. 58.22: nēmō nostrum est īdem māne quī fuit prīdiē
Verg. A. 5.305: nēmō ex hōc numerō
terms.comment: For persons, with a genitive or ex for the group: nēmō nostrum, none of us; nēmō ex hōc numerō, none of this number. Lewis & Short: classical Latin supplies the genitive and ablative from nūllīus, nūllō.

phrases.latin: quia mē vestīgia terrent, omnia tē adversum spectantia, nūlla retrōrsum
phrases.english: because the footprints frighten me: all of them pointing towards you, none coming back

phrases.latin: ‘nūllae, quod sciam,’ ille, ‘sed hīc piscārī nūllī solent’
phrases.english: (Was it some fishermen’s holiday?) ‘None that I know of,’ said he, ‘but nobody fishes here’

phrases.latin: utrumque enim vitium est, et omnibus crēdere et nūllī
phrases.english: for both are faults, to trust everyone and to trust none

phrases.latin: Quī omnēs īnsidiās timet, in nūllās incidit.
phrases.english: Whoever fears every trap falls into none.

phrases.latin: nēmō nostrum est īdem māne quī fuit prīdiē
phrases.english: none of us is the same in the morning as he was the day before

sources: Lewis & Short: nullus · Lewis & Short: nemo
